title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.

report.summary: InfraDev benchmark reveals top coding agents solve only 38.9% of real multi-GPU AI infrastructure tasks, exposing blind spots in tests.
report.background: AI infrastructure code — distributed training, inference serving, and reinforcement learning — is increasingly a target for coding agents, but evaluating them is hard. Existing benchmarks often focus on single kernels or single-GPU tasks and rely on official tests or prompt-based grading, which can pass incorrect patches and fail correct ones. InfraDev addresses this by drawing 36 tasks from real pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl. Each task requires reimplementing a multi-file change that must run correctly across many GPUs. The benchmark also introduces hidden probes synthesized to enforce requirements official tests miss, plus a prompt that states interfaces without revealing the solution. A shared execution environment reuses dependencies and artifacts to make multi-GPU evaluation practical. The result is a more realistic stress test for whether coding agents can develop production-grade AI infrastructure, not just isolated code snippets.
key_points: InfraDev is built from 36 real pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl. It covers training, inference, and reinforcement-learning infrastructure, and each task asks an agent to reimplement a multi-file change that must run correctly across many GPUs. This makes it closer to production engineering than single-kernel or single-GPU benchmarks.

Grading combines hidden probes with an interface-only prompt. The probes check requirements that official tests leave unchecked, and the prompt lists every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. The probes rejected 32% of submissions that passed all official tests, showing that conventional test-based grading can overstate agent performance.

Frontier coding agents struggle. Across six models, the best resolved only 38.9% of tasks. When given the original pull-request descriptions as prompts, no model resolved a single task. Failure analysis found structural and state errors dominate, and agents' self-written tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic.

The shared execution environment is an engineering contribution. By reusing dependencies and build artifacts across tasks, it cuts storage by 52–57% and build time by 13–14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. That makes repeated multi-GPU evaluation more feasible for researchers and teams.

Failure analysis can feed back into agent design. Turning the findings into an agent skill raised a frontier model's resolved rate on Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%. The result suggests that targeted guidance about structural correctness and resource constraints can improve coding agents without changing the underlying model.
report.impact: InfraDev raises the bar for evaluating coding agents on AI infrastructure. It shows that passing existing tests is not enough: hidden probes and multi-GPU execution expose structural, state, and resource-related errors that official tests miss. For the AI industry, this matters because training and serving stacks are expensive and failure-prone; agents that edit them need stronger verification. For developers, the lesson is to invest in hidden tests, multi-GPU CI, and agent skills that explicitly check memory, time, and traffic. For regular users, better evaluation should translate into more reliable model serving and training behind AI products, though the benchmark also signals that fully autonomous infrastructure development remains far from solved.
report.tools: Follow the InfraDev benchmark (arXiv:2610.36589) and the target repositories: Megatron-LM for training, vLLM for inference serving, and verl for reinforcement learning. Developers can reproduce tasks with multi-GPU CI, add hidden probes for memory, time, and traffic, and test coding agents against interface-only prompts. Watch distributed test harnesses and agent-skill libraries; these are likely to matter more than single-kernel benchmarks.
